refs.description: Criminal threats against domestic violence counselors and shelter staff — companion provision extending § 422 protections to victim advocates.

Dissuading a witness — overlaps with § 422 where the threat is intended to prevent a witness from reporting or testifying. Elements differ: § 136.1 focuses on preventing testimony; § 422 on causing sustained fear of violence.
Stalking — often charged in conjunction with § 422 where repeated threats form part of a stalking pattern. Distinct offense but shares 'credible threat' language that draws from § 422 doctrine.
Corporal injury to spouse/cohabitant — frequently charged alongside § 422 in domestic violence matters. Relevant to the steward's cases where family law and criminal cross-reference.

Conspiracy — where multiple actors coordinated to make or facilitate criminal threats as part of a larger scheme, conspiracy liability under § 182 can attach to all participants. Directly relevant to the multi-actor orchestration in the steward's cases.
Convicted felon prohibited from possessing firearms — a § 422 felony conviction triggers this prohibition. Sentencing consequence for steward-as-defendant track.
Jury instruction for criminal threats under § 422. The UUIS test from Toledo is codified in CALCRIM 1300. Defense counsel should review the instruction to identify missing element arguments.

Domestic violence restraining order — where a § 422 criminal threat is the predicate act, it supports a DVRO application. The threat analysis under § 422 informs the 'disturb the peace' and 'reasonable apprehension' standards in family court.

Mental health diversion — available for § 422 unless the specific conduct falls within an excluded category. A wobbler § 422 charge may qualify for diversion. Cross-reference the eligibility analysis in pen_code_1001_36_mental_health_diversion.

General misdemeanor diversion — where § 422 is charged as a misdemeanor (wobbler reduction), § 1001.95 general diversion is available as a backup if § 1001.36 is unavailable. Cross-reference pen_code_1001_95_misdemeanor_diversion.

True threats doctrine — the First Amendment does not protect 'true threats.' Virginia v. Black (2003) 538 U.S. 343 and Counterman v. Colorado (2023) 600 U.S. 66 (requiring subjective awareness of threatening nature). California's § 422 must be read consistently with the First Amendment true threats doctrine.

Discovery — in any § 422 prosecution, Brady/Giglio obligations apply. The call logs, communications metadata, and prior threat history are all subject to § 1054.1 disclosure. Cross-reference pen_code_1054_1_discovery.
